books.section: Topic 3.13 Continuity and Change in Period 3

primary_sources: Alexander Hamilton, Report on Manufactures, December 5, 1791

stimulus.text:
Alexander Hamilton, Report on Manufactures, December 5, 1791:

“Not only the wealth; but the independence and security of a Country, appear to be materially connected with the prosperity of manufactures. Every nation, with a view to those great objects, ought to endeavour to possess within itself all the essentials of national supply. These comprise the means of Subsistence habitation clothing and defence.”
stimulus.source_note: Alexander Hamilton, Report on Manufactures, December 5, 1791. Founders Online, National Archives. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus quoted from Alexander Hamilton, Report on Manufactures, December 5, 1791, public domain.
stem: Hamilton urged manufactures in 1791, yet in 1800 most Americans still farmed and lived in the countryside. What does that contrast best show?

options.text: Hamilton's report was ignored entirely and changed nothing at all.
options.misconception: Congress adopted much of the report, and manufactures did begin to grow.

options.text: Change came slowly: vision outran most Americans' farming life.
Farming ended in the United States during the 1790s.
options.misconception: Most Americans still farmed in 1800, so farming had not ended.

options.text: The United States became a manufacturing nation by 1800.
options.misconception: The country was still rural in 1800; manufactures came later.

rationales.A: Congress adopted much of the report, and manufactures did begin to grow.
rationales.B: Hamilton's 1791 vision called for factories, yet most Americans still farmed, so the plan ran ahead of daily life.
rationales.C: Most Americans still farmed in 1800, so farming had not ended.
rationales.D: The country was still rural in 1800; manufactures came later.
rationales.general:
1. Hamilton's 1791 report urged the nation to make its own goods.
2. Background: in 1790 the five largest cities held only about 110,000 of nearly 4 million people, so most Americans lived on farms.
3. By 1800 that farming life still held: manufactures had begun, but the country was still rural.
4. So the government's vision ran ahead of daily life.
Remember: a plan and a practice are two different things, so check the numbers.
